CHAPTER XLVIII

Catherine was in dismay when she reflected that Gerard must reach home
in another month at farthest, more likely in a week; and how should she
tell him she had not even kept an eye upon his betrothed? Then there was
the uncertainty as to the girl's fate; and this uncertainty sometimes
took a sickening form.

“Oh, Kate,” she groaned, “if she should have gone and made herself
away!”

“Mother, she would never be so wicked.”

“Ah, my lass, you know not what hasty fools young lasses be, that have
no mothers to keep 'em straight. They will fling themselves into the
water for a man that the next man they meet would ha' cured 'em of in a
week. I have known 'em to jump in like brass one moment and scream for
help in the next. Couldn't know their own minds ye see even about such
a trifle as yon. And then there's times when their bodies ail like no
other living creatures ever I could hear of, and that strings up their
feelings so, the patience, that belongs to them at other times beyond
all living souls barring an ass, seems all to jump out of 'em at
one turn, and into the water they go. Therefore, I say that men are
monsters.”

“Mother!”

“Monsters, and no less, to go making such heaps o' canals just to tempt
the poor women in. They know we shall not cut our throats, hating the
sight of blood and rating our skins a hantle higher nor our lives; and
as for hanging, while she is a fixing of the nail and a making of the
noose she has time t' alter her mind. But a jump into a canal is no more
than into bed; and the water it does all the lave, will ye, nill ye.
Why, look at me, the mother o' nine, wasn't I agog to make a hole in our
canal for the nonce?”

“Nay, mother, I'll never believe it of you.”

“Ye may, though. 'Twas in the first year of our keeping house together.
Eli hadn't found out my weak stitches then, nor I his; so we made a
rent, pulling contrariwise; had a quarrel. So then I ran crying, to tell
some gabbling fool like myself what I had no business to tell out o'
doors except to the saints, and there was one of our precious canals in
the way; do they take us for teal? Oh, how tempting it did look! Says I
to myself, 'Sith he has let me go out of his door quarrelled, he shall
see me drowned next, and then he will change his key. He will blubber
a good one, and I shall look down from heaven' (I forgot I should be in
t'other part), 'and see him take on, and oh, but that will be sweet!'
and I was all a tiptoe and going in, only just then I thought I
wouldn't. I had got a new gown a making, for one thing, and hard upon
finished. So I went home instead, and what was Eli's first word, 'Let
yon flea stick i' the wall, my lass,' says he. 'Not a word of all I said
t' anger thee was sooth, but this, “I love thee.”' These were his very
words; I minded 'em, being the first quarrel. So I flung my arms about
his neck and sobbed a bit, and thought o' the canal; and he was no
colder to me than I to him, being a man and a young one; and so then
that was better than lying in the water; and spoiling my wedding kirtle
and my fine new shoon, old John Bush made 'em, that was uncle to him
keeps the shop now. And what was my grief to hers?”

Little Kate hoped that Margaret loved her father too much to think of
leaving him so at his age. “He is father and mother and all to her, you
know.”

“Nay, Kate, they do forget all these things in a moment o' despair when
the very sky seems black above them. I place more faith in him that
is unborn, than on him that is ripe for the grave, to keep her out o'
mischief. For certes it do go sore against us to die when there's a
little innocent a pulling at our hearts to let 'un live, and feeding at
our very veins.”

“Well, then, keep up a good heart, mother.” She added, that very likely
all these fears were exaggerated. She ended by solemnly entreating her
mother at all events not to persist in naming the sex of Margaret's
infant. It was so unlucky, all the gossips told her; “dear heart, as if
there were not as many girls born as boys.”

This reflection, though not unreasonable, was met with clamour.

“Have you the cruelty to threaten me with a girl!!? I want no more
girls, while I have you. What use would a lass be to me? Can I set her
on my knee and see my Gerard again as I can a boy? I tell thee 'tis all
settled.

“How may that be?”

“In my mind. And if I am to be disappointed i' the end, 'tisn't for you
to disappoint me beforehand, telling me it is not to be a child, but
only a girl.”

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER TWO.
[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"O God! It's all over with me," said he at last. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What's the matter, master?" said I.
[Reference Rewrite]: I left him in the dark, initiating a careful descent down the rain-slicked precipices that formed the carceral walls of our world. Before I had traversed fifty paces, a sudden rupture of lightning tore the sky, pursued instantly by a shriek so guttural it arrested my breath. It was a sound stripped of all former sovereignty. I could not trace its origin through the howling wind, but then I heard the voice—his voice, diminished and frantic—commanding my return.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

In that interim, how was she to confess the terrible truth—that she had failed to watch over his betrothed? The uncertainty regarding the girl's fate hung over them like a storm cloud, occasionally coalescing into a sickening, tangible horror. "Oh, Kate," she groaned, her voice trembling, "what if she has already thrown herself into the water?" Her mother's response was immediate, cutting through the silence with the blunt wisdom of experience. "Margaret would never be so wicked," Catherine protested, clinging to the hope of her friend's virtue. "Ah, my lass, you know not the chaotic nature of young women unmoored from maternal guidance," her mother replied, her tone shifting from comfort to grim warning. "They are capable of throwing themselves into the depths for a man whom the next stranger might cure in a single week. I have seen them leap into the canal with the resolve of iron, only to scream for mercy moments later, unable to command their own minds even over such trifles. Worse still, there are times when their bodies ail in ways unknown to any other creature, stringing their emotions so tightly that the patience inherent in their souls vanishes entirely, sending them plunging into the water without a second thought. Thus, I declare that men are monsters." "Mother!" Catherine cried out, recoiling at the accusation. "Monsters, and no less," her mother insisted, her eyes hardening. "They construct these very canals merely to tempt poor women. They know we possess no desire to cut our throats, nor do we rate our skin or our lives so highly that we would willingly spill blood. As for hanging, while she waits for the nail to be fixed and the noose to be fashioned, she retains the luxury of changing her mind. But a jump into a canal is akin to jumping into bed; the water does all the work, whether you wish it or not." The mother paused, her gaze drifting to the window as if recalling a distant memory. "Consider me, the mother of nine. Was I not once eager to make a hole in our canal right here and now?" "Nay, Mother, I shall never believe you capable of such folly." "You may believe it, though," her mother countered, a wry smile touching her lips. "It happened in the first year of our household. Eli had not yet discovered my weak stitches, nor I his; we pulled in contrary directions until we made a rent in our peace. I ran crying to a gossiping fool like myself, sharing secrets meant only for the saints, and lo, one of our precious canals lay directly in my path. Did they take us for teal? How tempting it looked! I told myself, 'Since he has allowed me to leave his door in a quarrel, he shall see me drowned next, and then he will change his key. He will weep a proper flood, and I shall look down from heaven—and yes, I forgot I should be elsewhere—watch him mourn, and oh, that would be sweet indeed.' My feet were already dancing on the edge, ready to plunge, until suddenly I stopped." She shook her head, the image fading. "I had a new gown in progress, nearly finished, and I chose to go home instead. What was Eli's first word upon seeing me? 'Let that flea stick in the wall, my lass,' he said. 'Not a word of what angered you was true, save this: I love thee.' Those were his exact words, spoken during our first quarrel. I remembered them, and I flung my arms around his neck, sobbing briefly, thinking of the canal. He was no colder to me than I to him, being a man and a youth; the warmth returned between us. That embrace was infinitely sweeter than lying in the freezing water, saving my wedding kirtle and the fine new shoes crafted by old John Bush, his uncle who still runs the shop today. And what was my grief compared to hers?" Little Kate pressed forward, hoping that Margaret's love for her aging father would anchor her. "He is father, mother, and everything to her, you know." "Nay, Kate," her mother dismissed gently, "they forget all such bonds in a moment of despair when the sky itself turns black above them. I place greater faith in the unborn than in him who is ripe for the grave to keep her from mischief. For truly, it goes sore against our nature to die when a little innocent pulls at our hearts, begging to live, feeding upon our very veins." "Very well, then, keep your heart high, Mother," Catherine urged, adding internally that these fears were likely exaggerated. She concluded by solemnly entreating her mother to cease naming the sex of Margaret's infant. It was considered unluckily superstitious, a notion reinforced by every gossip in town. "Dear heart, as if there were not as many girls born as boys," she reasoned. Yet this reflection, though logically sound, met with a clamorous rejection. "Do you possess the cruelty to threaten me with a girl?!" her mother exclaimed, her composure fracturing. "I want no more girls while I have you. What use would a lass be to me? Can I sit her on my knee and see my Gerard again as I can with a boy? I tell thee, it is all settled." "How can that be?" Catherine asked, bewildered. "In my mind," her mother declared firmly. "And if I am to be disappointed in the end, it is not for you to disappoint me beforehand by telling me it cannot be a child, but only a girl."
